Non-ELLs scored about the same on both item types, so the visual items are not easier. Removing them would make the test less valid for ELLs.

Using more visual items is reasonable, but students still need scaffolded practice with text-based items. The data support a conclusion about what the text-heavy items measured, not dropping them entirely.

questions.key: If ELLs succeed on visual items but not on text-heavy items covering the same content, the text-heavy items are measuring language.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the main purpose of reducing the linguistic load of a content-area assessment for ELLs?
options: To minimize construct-irrelevant language demands so the assessment measures the intended content knowledge.
To lower the content standard being assessed so that a greater number of ELLs are able to earn passing scores.
To give ELLs practice with simplified English that will help prepare them for the NYSESLAT.
To eliminate the need for testing accommodations such as extended time and bilingual glossaries.
questions.why: Every content assessment targets a construct, such as understanding heat transfer or the causes of a war. Complex language that is not part of that construct (long sentences, unfamiliar idioms, unnecessary words) adds construct-irrelevant variance, so scores reflect English proficiency as well as content. Reducing the linguistic load improves validity for ELLs while the content standard stays the same.

traps.note: Reducing the linguistic load changes the language, not the content standard. Lowering the standard would make the test measure something easier.
The NYSESLAT measures English proficiency, while a content assessment measures content knowledge. Linguistic modification serves the content construct, not language-test preparation.
Clear language and accommodations work together. Even well-modified items may call for extended time or a glossary for some ELLs.

questions.key: Reduce construct-irrelevant language so content assessments measure content, not English proficiency; keep the standard the same.

lessons.title: Teaching Social Studies to ELLs
lessons.why: Field 116 gives you a history text, map, timeline, or primary source and asks which language feature trips up ELLs, or which scaffold keeps grade-level social studies thinking accessible.

body.h: Why social studies is so language-heavy
body.md:
Social studies may be the most language-dependent content area. Math has numbers and symbols, and science has hands-on labs, but history and civics are carried almost entirely by text and talk. ELLs face several layers at once:

- **Abstract concepts** (democracy, federalism, imperialism, sovereignty) that are hard to show in a picture.
- **Assumed background knowledge**: textbooks take for granted that readers know U.S. geography, holidays, and political symbols.
- **Dense, context-reduced text** full of nominalizations (the expansion of the railroads), cause-effect chains, and long sentences.
- **Everyday words with civic meanings**: cabinet, party, bill, run (for office), branch, state, court, depression.

In Cummins's terms, a social studies textbook is cognitively demanding and context-reduced, the hardest combination. On the exam, the best answer almost always adds context and scaffolds while keeping the thinking at grade level. Answers that swap the primary source for a summary, or postpone the unit until students are "ready," are traps.

body.h: Chronology: order of mention is not order of events
body.md:
History texts rarely tell events in order. Consider: "Families settled western New York after the Erie Canal had opened in 1825; before that, crops had been hauled by wagon." The settlers are mentioned first, but they came last. Many ELLs use an **order-of-mention** strategy, so teach the signals explicitly:

- **Temporal connectives**: before, after, prior to, by the time, until, meanwhile, subsequently.
- **The past perfect** (had opened) marks the earlier of two past events.
- **Century names**: the 1700s are the eighteenth century. Spanish siglo XVIII follows the same rule, which makes a useful bridge. Also teach decades (the 1920s), circa, and B.C.E./C.E.

**Classroom moves:** students number the events in a complex sentence and then place them on a timeline. Entering students sequence picture cards with dates and captions and answer "What happened first? Next?" by pointing or naming.

body.h: Cause and effect, stated and implied
body.md:
Cause-effect reasoning is the backbone of history, and it shows up in three ways:

- **Signaled**: because, as a result, consequently, led to, therefore, due to.
- **Packed into nouns and verbs**: "The resulting decline in trade forced Parliament to repeal the act."
- **Implied**: "In 1845, a disease began destroying Ireland's potato crop. Over the next decade, more than a million people left." No connective links the two sentences. Readers must infer the link, and ELLs who hunt for "because" may say the text gives no reason.

**Classroom moves:** model the inference aloud, have students rewrite implied links with because or as a result, and match the organizer to the structure. Use a chain for a sequence of causes, and a multiple-cause diagram when several causes (militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism) lead to one effect (World War I). A Venn diagram is built for comparison, not causation.

Primary sources are non-negotiable in social studies, so **scaffold, don't substitute**:

- **Excerpt** (shorten without rewriting), read aloud, and **gloss** key words in the margin.
- Ask **sourcing questions**: Who wrote it? When? For what audience? Why?
- Have pairs paraphrase each chunk before analyzing the argument.

Visual sources lower the language load, but they are not automatically comprehensible. A political cartoon of an octopus labeled "Standard Oil" only works if you know what the octopus symbolizes and what a monopoly is. Teach the symbols and context, then guide students with "What do you see? What might it stand for? What is the cartoonist's point of view?" Remember that a cartoon published during the period it comments on is a **primary** source.

**Maps** carry their own language: prepositions of location (north of, bordered by, between), legends, scale, and physical vs. political maps. Entering students can show real understanding by color-coding a physical map and completing a frame such as "People lived near the ___ because ___" in English or the home language.

body.h: Background knowledge, funds of knowledge, and multiple perspectives
body.md:
Build background by **connecting to what students already know**, never by assuming they know nothing. Before a unit on the three branches of government, have students discuss, in any language, who makes, enforces, and judges rules in their families, schools, and home countries, then link those ideas to a labeled visual. **Simulations**, such as paying "taxes" without a vote, make abstract ideas context-embedded without lowering cognitive demand.

**Funds of knowledge** (Moll) means the knowledge in students' households and communities. An oral-history interview with a family or community member of the student's choosing, compared with Ellis Island–era primary sources, turns that knowledge into historical analysis. Contrast this with asking each ELL to present "the customs of my country," which tokenizes students and stereotypes cultures.

**Multiple perspectives** is both a social studies skill and a CR-SE principle (inclusive curriculum). Pair contrasting sources, such as Jackson's 1830 message to Congress and a Cherokee petition, and give frames like "From the perspective of ___, the policy was ___ because ___."

The content and the thinking stay the same at every level; the language support changes:

- **Entering**: picture-card timelines, labeling and color-coding maps, sorting cause/effect picture cards, one-word or phrase answers, home-language responses.
- **Emerging**: simple frames ("___ caused ___"), word banks, partner talk with visuals, short glossed excerpts.
- **Transitioning**: perspective charts, paraphrasing primary-source chunks, frames with because, although, and as a result.
- **Expanding**: document-based arguments with frames that link evidence to a claim ("According to Document 2, ___. This shows that ___ because ___"), hedged claims, and comparison of sources.

When Expanding students list facts without explaining them, the fix is targeted: model how a writer connects evidence to a claim. Don't fall back on a list of transition words, and don't let them skip the essay.

traps: Exam trap: replacing a primary source with a textbook summary, or a hard concept with an easier topic. That lowers rigor; scaffold the original instead.
Exam trap: assuming visuals (cartoons, photos, maps) explain themselves. They rely on cultural symbols and background knowledge that must be taught.
Exam trap: blaming a sequencing or cause-effect error on L1 transfer or a disability when the text's chronology or causal language explains it.
Exam trap: asking ELLs to represent their whole culture ("tell us about your country's holidays"). Funds of knowledge draws on real household knowledge tied to the content.
Exam trap: choosing a Venn diagram or a timeline for a cause-effect text. Match the organizer to the text structure.

terms.d: The order in which events appear in a sentence; in history texts it often differs from the order in which they happened.
Had + past participle (had opened); marks the earlier of two past events and signals chronology.
A word or phrase showing time relationships: before, after, prior to, by the time, subsequently.
A cause-effect link the reader must infer because no signal word such as because or as a result states it.
Organizer showing several causes leading to one effect, such as the long-term causes of World War I.
A document or artifact created during the period studied: a speech, letter, photograph, or cartoon of the time.
A later interpretation by someone who did not experience the events, such as a textbook or encyclopedia article.
Asking who created a source, when, for what audience, and why, before interpreting its content.
Shortening a primary source while keeping the author's original words; a scaffold, not a simplification.
Adding brief marginal explanations or translations of key words to a text.
Examining an event through sources from people with different positions, purposes, and experiences.
Moll's term for the knowledge and skills in students' households and communities, used as curricular resources.
Cummins: supported by concrete cues such as visuals, experience, and interaction; simulations make demanding concepts context-embedded.
Everyday words with special social studies meanings: cabinet, party, bill, run, branch, court.

lessons.tip: In social studies items, the option that keeps the original source or concept and adds visuals, frames, or interaction usually beats simplifying, lecturing, or postponing.

lessons.title: Academic Language Across the Disciplines
lessons.why: Field 116 shows you a sentence, passage, or set of frames and asks you to name the feature (nominalization, a concessive connective, a text structure, a language function) that challenges ELLs, and to choose the scaffold that addresses it.

body.md:
Academic language is much more than hard vocabulary. Think of it at three levels:

- **Word/phrase**: general academic (Tier 2) words such as analyze, evidence, significant, factor, and structure; discipline-specific (Tier 3) words such as photosynthesis and legislature; and everyday words with special meanings (table, product, party, cabinet).
- **Sentence**: complex sentences, embedded clauses, appositives, passive voice, and nominalizations.
- **Discourse**: how a whole text is organized (text structure) and held together (signal words, reference chains).

Students move along a **register continuum** from everyday talk ("the ice go water more fast") to academic writing ("the ice melted faster because dark surfaces absorb more light"). The best teacher moves affirm the idea, recast it academically, and give a frame for the next step. Don't reject the everyday version, and don't make students wait until they "know the words."

body.h: Language functions and the forms they need
body.md:
A **language function** is what students do with language. Each function calls for particular forms, and a good language objective names both:

- **Describe**: adjectives, prepositional phrases, relative clauses ("a mineral that is…").
- **Sequence**: first, then, after, finally; past tense; time clauses.
- **Compare/contrast**: -er than, both… and, whereas, while, unlike, similarly.
- **Explain (cause/effect)**: because, so, as a result, which causes, led to.
- **Argue**: a claim (I believe), evidence (the data show), concession and rebuttal (Although some claim…; however…), and hedges.

Example: the content objective is "Compare mammals and reptiles"; the language objective is "Compare orally with a partner using whereas, both… and, and unlike." On the exam, watch for options that only name an activity ("read the chapter") or a form that doesn't fit the function (past tense in a compare lesson).

**Hedging** is an advanced argue skill: academic writers fit claims to evidence (suggests, indicates, may, in this experiment). A student who writes "Our data proves heat always makes every reaction faster" needs a mini-lesson on hedging, not on sequence words.

Most informational texts use five structures. Signal words reveal them, and a matching organizer makes them visible:

- **Description**: for example, such as, characteristics include. Organizer: web.
- **Sequence/chronology**: first, next, before, after, in 1825. Organizer: timeline or flowchart.
- **Compare/contrast**: both, whereas, in contrast, unlike, similarly. Organizer: Venn diagram or comparison chart.
- **Cause/effect**: because, as a result, consequently, led to. Organizer: cause-effect chain or multiple-cause diagram.
- **Problem/solution**: one problem, to address this, in response, a solution. Organizer: problem → solution → result.

Real texts mix structures, so look for the **overall** one. A passage about smog and the Clean Air Act contains cause and effect, but "To address this problem" and "In response" make it problem/solution as a whole.

Two high-yield traps involve signals. **Concessive connectives** (despite, although, even though, nevertheless) introduce an unexpected contrast, not a cause: a student who summarizes "Despite plenty of rain, the crop failed because of insects" as "it failed because of rain" misread the word despite. And **implied relationships** have no signal at all, so students must infer them.

**Nominalization** turns verbs or adjectives into nouns: erode → erosion, expand → expansion, productive → productivity. Compare:

- Everyday: "When farmers cut down the forests, the soil washed away, and the land couldn't grow crops."
- Academic: "Rapid deforestation caused severe soil erosion and a decline in agricultural productivity."

The academic version is shorter but denser. It packs whole events into noun phrases, removes the people doing the actions, and links processes with one verb (caused). Writers use nominalization to condense information, to treat processes as things that can be measured or evaluated, and to connect ideas across sentences ("This expansion…").

Don't confuse it with the **passive voice** ("the forests were cut down"). The passive keeps the verb; nominalization turns the verb into a noun.

**Teach it by unpacking and repacking.** Unpack the noun phrase into who-did-what clauses ("Railroads expanded rapidly. River towns declined."), discuss how the ideas connect, and then have students repack ideas into noun phrases in their own writing. Rewriting texts to remove nominalizations lowers rigor, and a verb-to-noun worksheet is isolated practice.

**Embedded clauses** can separate a subject from its verb: "The colonists who refused to buy goods that Parliament had taxed hoped to pressure British merchants." A student who answers "Parliament" to "Who hoped?" took the noun nearest the verb. **Sentence deconstruction** (often called working with a "juicy sentence") fixes this: chunk the sentence, find the main subject and verb (colonists… hoped), and ask what each clause tells about which noun. A few minutes a day with one rich sentence from the day's text builds syntactic awareness.

**Appositives** define terms inside the sentence: "The Haudenosaunee Confederacy, an alliance of Indigenous nations, …" Teach students that the phrase between the commas renames the noun. Similar definition signals include which is, called, also known as, and that is.

**Reference chains** hold texts together: "Rain washed fertilizer into the lake. There, it caused algae to grow. When the algae died, bacteria decomposed them. This process used up the oxygen." Summarizing phrases such as this process or these changes can point back to a whole sentence. Have students draw arrows from each referring word to what it refers to, then retell the chain.

body.h: General academic vocabulary and differentiation by level
body.md:
**Tier 2 general academic words** (analyze, evidence, significant, structure, factor, process, interpret) appear in every subject and in test directions, yet teachers often assume students already know them. A schoolwide set taught across content areas gives the biggest return. Tier 3 words (isotope, tariff) are taught within their discipline, and Tier 1 words (house, walk) are mostly acquired through daily use.

**Differentiate the language, not the task.** For a lesson comparing Mesopotamia and Egypt:

- Emerging: "Mesopotamia had ___. Egypt had ___." with a word bank and visuals.
- Expanding: "While Mesopotamia ___, Egypt ___, which suggests that ___."

Everyone does the same comparison, and the scaffolds decrease as proficiency grows, just as the NLAP shows each standard at five levels.

traps: Exam trap: calling a dense academic sentence "passive" when it is actually nominalized. Check whether the verb became a noun (erosion) or stayed a verb (was eroded).
Exam trap: judging difficulty by length. Nominalized sentences are often shorter but harder.
Exam trap: reading although, however, or despite as plain contrast or as a cause. In arguments they mark concession and rebuttal, and despite never introduces the cause.
Exam trap: stripping complex language out of texts (no nominalizations, no pronouns) instead of teaching students to unpack it.
Exam trap: a "language objective" that is only an activity, or whose forms don't match the function (past tense in a compare lesson).

terms.d: The purpose for using language in a task: describe, sequence, compare, explain, argue.
The grammar and vocabulary that carry out a function, such as whereas and -er than for comparing.
A word or phrase that reveals relationships and text structure: because, in contrast, first, to address this problem.
The overall organization of a text: description, sequence, compare/contrast, cause/effect, or problem/solution.
Despite, although, even though, nevertheless: introduces something contrary to expectation, not a cause.
Turning a verb or adjective into a noun (erode → erosion), condensing a process into a dense, agentless noun phrase.
Rewriting a dense noun phrase as clauses that show who did what, revealing meaning and relationships.
A clause inside another clause (who refused…, that Parliament had taxed) that modifies a noun.
Chunking a complex sentence to find the main clause and see how the other parts modify it; also called juicy sentences.
A noun phrase set off by commas that renames or defines the noun right before it.
A series of pronouns and summarizing nouns (it, them, this process) that point back to earlier ideas.
Language that qualifies a claim to fit the evidence: suggests, may, likely, in this experiment.
A general academic word used across disciplines (analyze, significant, factor); high priority for explicit teaching.
The range from everyday spoken language to formal written academic language; teachers bridge students along it.

lessons.tip: Name the feature first (nominalization? concessive? embedded clause? text structure?), then pick the option that teaches students to unpack that feature in grade-level text.

lessons.title: Assessing Content Learning of ELLs
lessons.why: Field 116 shows you a test, rubric, student response, or data table and asks whether it measures content or English, and which change makes the assessment valid without lowering the standard.

body.h: The one big idea: what is this assessment measuring?
body.md:
Every content assessment targets a **construct**: understanding heat transfer, the causes of the Civil War, solving two-step equations. For ELLs, language that is not part of that construct (long sentences, unfamiliar contexts, essay formats) adds **construct-irrelevant variance**, so the score partly reflects English proficiency instead of content knowledge. That is a **validity** problem.

Example: Hamid, an Emerging ELL, scores 45% on a two-essay Civil War test, yet he sorts cause/effect cards correctly, explains the Fugitive Slave Act with a frame, and keeps an accurate organizer. The essay test measured his English writing. Adding more essay questions would make the test more reliable (consistent) but no more valid for him.

- **Validity**: Does it measure what it claims to measure?
- **Reliability**: Does it measure consistently?
- **Bias**: Does something irrelevant to the construct, such as culture or language, disadvantage a group?

When an exam item shows test results that clash with other evidence, the answer is almost always that the format masked content knowledge.

body.h: Reducing the language load without lowering the standard
body.md:
**Linguistic modification** rewrites items to remove unnecessary language while keeping the concept and format:

- Short, active sentences instead of long, embedded, or passive ones.
- Familiar, concrete contexts instead of culturally loaded ones (innings and at-bats → pages and minutes).
- Remove irrelevant words and clauses, but keep essential content vocabulary.
- Add visuals or labeled diagrams that support, rather than supply, the content.

Compare "Which of the following would most likely be observed by a student who, after carefully placing a healthy plant in a closet where it would not be exposed to any light…" with "A healthy plant is kept in a dark closet for two weeks. What will most likely happen to its leaves?"

Watch for over-modification that changes the construct:

- **Giving the answer away**: adding a definition of photosynthesis, or printing a worked example beside each item.
- **Lowering the standard**: one-step equations instead of two-step, or below-grade vocabulary tests.
- **Changing the format**: yes/no items invite guessing.
- **Deleting the word problems** when the standard requires applying math to real-world situations.

body.h: Performance tasks and other ways to show knowledge
body.md:
Students at lower proficiency levels can show sophisticated content knowledge when the response mode fits:

- **Entering**: sort, sequence, label, draw, build, demonstrate, or point to a diagram; answer in the home language; give one-word or phrase answers with a word bank.
- **Emerging**: labeled diagrams with short frames, oral explanations with visuals, cloze summaries.
- **Transitioning and Expanding**: written explanations and arguments with frames, graphic organizers, and analytic rubrics.

**Home-language responses** are powerful for students with strong prior schooling. A newcomer from Ecuador with high biology grades can write her answers in Spanish, with a qualified bilingual educator helping to score them. NYS also allows ELLs to write responses to state content-test items in the home language.

**Formative checks** should let every student respond with little language: picture cards held up or arranged on whiteboards, gestures tied to specific choices, quick partner explanations. "Does everyone understand?" gives no valid information.

For SIFE and Entering students, use **multiple measures over time** (maps, observation checklists, photos of hands-on products, oral interviews with visuals, with a bilingual staff member if possible) rather than one English test.

Use **analytic rubrics** that score content and language as separate criteria, for example scientific explanation, scientific vocabulary, and language conventions. They keep developing grammar from dragging down the content score, and they show exactly where a student needs support. A **holistic** rubric gives one overall impression, so language problems can lower the whole score. Rubrics are **criterion-referenced**: work is compared with standards, not with classmates.

Score the construct. Jae-won writes, "Metal is take the heat fast from air. Plastic no take heat fast. So ice on metal get more heat, melt more fast." The science is correct, so he earns content credit, and the grammar gets separate language feedback. Omitted articles are typical for Emerging ELLs (Korean has no articles) and are not a sign of a disability.

Share rubrics in advance, in student-friendly language with exemplars, and use them for self-assessment.

**Report card grades** should reflect mastery of the same grade-level standards, shown through scaffolded tasks. Avoid effort-only grades, identical unsupported tests, and a blank grade with only a NYSESLAT level.

Know the NYS rules, because items test them:

- **Bilingual glossaries** must be **word-to-word**, with no definitions, pictures, or explanations.
- Glossaries, translated editions (math, science, social studies), oral translation for lower-incidence languages, and writing responses in the home language apply to **content tests only, never ELA**.
- Extended time (for example, time and a half) and a separate location or small group are also available.
- **Former ELLs** keep their testing accommodations for **2 years** after exiting.

Good classroom practice mirrors the state rules: students use word-to-word glossaries regularly during instruction and classroom tests, so the tool is familiar and classroom scores reflect content the same way state scores do. Withholding glossaries in class "to see what they can do alone" makes classroom scores less valid and leaves students unpracticed. A glossary with definitions on a Regents science exam, or any glossary on the ELA Regents, violates policy.

Item analysis can reveal whether language is masking content. Suppose Transitioning ELLs score 80% on map-based items but 41% on text-heavy items about the same content, while non-ELLs score about the same on both. The best-supported conclusion is that the text-heavy items measured reading as well as content. Neither "reteach everything" nor "remove the map items" follows from those data. The sensible next steps are to revise the text-heavy items, keep multiple formats, and keep building students' reading of content text.

Also check for **cultural bias**: an item that depends on knowing baseball, U.S. holidays, or snow days tests that knowledge along with the target skill. Keep the math and change the context.

traps: Exam trap: treating a reliability fix (more items) as a validity fix. More essay questions still measure English writing.
Exam trap: "simplifying" a test by lowering the standard, adding content clues, or deleting word problems. Change the language, not the construct.
Exam trap: glossaries with definitions, or any glossary or translation on ELA tests. NYS allows word-to-word glossaries on content tests only.
Exam trap: excusing ELLs from assessment or grading them on effort. Assess grade-level content in accessible formats.
Exam trap: lowering a content score for grammar errors when the meaning is clear, or reading typical L2 errors as signs of a disability.

terms.d: The specific knowledge or skill an assessment is meant to measure.
Score differences caused by factors outside the construct, such as English proficiency on a science test.
The degree to which an assessment measures what it claims to measure and supports the decisions made from it.
The consistency of an assessment's results across items, scorers, and occasions.
Simplifying the language of test items (short active sentences, familiar contexts) without changing the tested concept.
An assessment in which students show knowledge by doing: labeling, sequencing, building, or demonstrating.
A rubric that scores separate criteria, such as content, vocabulary, and conventions, each on its own scale.
A rubric that gives one overall score based on a general impression of the work.
Compares performance with fixed standards or criteria rather than with other students.
A bilingual list of direct translations without definitions; the only glossary type NYS allows on state content tests.
Letting ELLs answer content items in the home language, which separates content knowledge from English proficiency.
Using several kinds of evidence over time (observation, products, oral, written) to judge learning.
An item feature that depends on cultural knowledge unrelated to the construct and so disadvantages some students.
Ongoing checks during instruction used to adjust teaching; for ELLs, ideally low-language responses from every student.

lessons.tip: For every 5.7 item ask, "Is this measuring the content or the English?" Pick the option that removes the language barrier while keeping the same standard.
